Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Sia was thirty-nine years old, a park ranger in a sprawling national forest in the Pacific Northwest, and she had been a relief worker once, in a war zone she could barely speak of now. That part of her life felt like it belonged to someone else, or to no one at all. The memory of it came to her not as a story but as a scent: a specific cologne, heavy and sweet, that would drift toward her without warning—from a visitor on a trail, from a stranger in a grocery store aisle—and then she would be gone, lost inside a moment she could not control. Her husband, Leo, had learned to approach her slowly, to announce himself before touching her, because even a hug could do it: the warmth of arms around her, meant as comfort, could suddenly feel like a trap closing in.

She could not tell anyone what had happened. Not Leo, not the chaplain she had tried to see once, not the therapist at the VA clinic she had driven to and then driven past three times before giving up. When she tried to explain, the thread would slip away. Some moments were impossibly clear—the dust in the light, the sound of a generator, the weight of her vest—and others were simply gone, erased as if they had never been. She had no coherent story, only fragments that did not fit together, and she had come to believe that this meant she was hiding something, even from herself. That she had done something in those blank spaces that she could not face.

She had been stationed in a city under siege, distributing food and water to families who had lost everything. She remembered the children most clearly. But she also remembered a checkpoint, a man in a uniform, the cologne he wore—something expensive and out of place—and then nothing. Then the next clear image: her hands, wet, and someone screaming. She did not know whose. She had never been able to fill in what came between.

In the years since, Sia had built a life around avoidance, though she did not call it that. She stopped going to church, even though she had once found solace there. The silence of the sanctuary felt accusatory now, and she was certain that if she walked through those doors, something in her would crack open. She avoided doctors, avoided anyone who might ask questions she could not answer. She had not had a physical in four years. When her supervisor suggested she see someone after a panic attack on the job, she had laughed it off and changed the subject.

Her work as a ranger had become a kind of refuge and a kind of prison. She knew every trail, every ridge, every turn of the river. She could read the forest the way she could not read her own mind. But she had also begun to avoid the parts of the park she did not know well—the backcountry routes, the new interpretive trails—because she could not assess the danger there. She had become hypervigilant on the job, watching visitors not for litter or fire risk but for threat. A sudden movement from a hiker stepping out from behind a tree would send her heart into her throat. She scanned crowds for anyone who moved wrong, who smelled wrong, who might be dangerous. She knew, logically, that she was safe. But she could not make her body believe it.

The most frightening thing, the thing she had never said aloud, was that she was not sure her life was worth living anymore. She had acted in ways that went against who she believed herself to be—she was certain of that, even if she could not remember the details. She no longer belonged anywhere. Not in the world of relief work, not in the quiet life she had tried to build, not even in her own skin. She went through the motions: she made dinner, she kissed Leo goodnight, she patrolled the trails. But she felt like a ghost in her own life.

What finally brought her to seek help was a small thing, or what seemed like a small thing. A child on a school field trip had run up to her and hugged her legs, thanking her for being a ranger. The scent of the child’s mother’s perfume had lingered in the air. Sia had frozen, then excused herself, then walked into the trees and vomited. That night, she told Leo she needed to talk to someone. She was terrified of what she might find if she did—the blank spaces filled in, the person she had been revealed—but she was more terrified of going on like this, a woman who could not be held, who could not tell her own story, who was disappearing piece by piece into the gaps.
